title: Video Clip - USFWS on Frog Rescue (23792856135)
description:
Video of Dr. Steven Detwiler discussing the need to save the endangered Mountain yellow-legged frog from a deadly fungal disease known as chytrid.
In the last 15 years, a fungal disease known as chytrid has led to the extinction or decline of over 200 species of frogs and salamanders, including species in our region.
The Service is partnering with the National Park Service, the San Francisco and Oakland Zoos and others to counter the rapid and severe decline of the Northern California Distinct Population Segment of mountain yellow-legged frogs.
The photos and video in this album represent one such effort.

More information is available at www.fws.gov/sacramento

transcript.text: I'm Stephen Detweiler with the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the Sacramento Fish and Wildlife Office.
We're very excited to be involved in this active restoration effort with the Mount
and Yellowgood Frog. If the Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Park Service and the zoos
had not acted when we did, there is a very high probability we would have lost these two critical
populations. So this active intervention has been key in now providing a chance to two
populations of a critically endangered species. Their chances of survival had we not done
this intervention were very low. At this life stage when they metamorphose, they're
most vulnerable to the catrud effects of catrudomicosis. So we expect we would have lost well over
90% to the disease. These individuals were about to metamorphose and it's hard to time
that and to know. So we had about a two-week notice of a window from Danny Boyano at Sequoia
Kings where we had to make sure everything was lined up, the schedule of the copter, the
kids, the person up from the zoos and make this all happen during an intense busy field
season. The Fish and Wildlife Service as we have a leadership role in the conservation
strategy development. So much of that involves the opportunity for me here who's mostly
at my desk to be able to help coordinate and facilitate permitting calls with a zoo if
it's needed, feeling calls from Danny from Sequoia Kings National Park who was very busy
dealing with fires and rescues and all kinds of things. And within all of that we were able
to get some helicopter time fortunately at the critical point where the frogs needed to
come out. The Fish and Wildlife Service is very excited to be involved in this effort.
It's an opportunity to actively restore an at-risk population and getting to see these
animals in the zoos was very fulfilling for me personally and it really brought home how
these interagency collaborative efforts can lead to successful restoration actions. We're
very grateful to all our partners who cooperated on this rescue effort. We're from the Park
Service who's done so much, volunteered their staff in time and to the zoos have completely
stepped up and donated their staff time and resources.
